The user asked for: **按照以下方向，生成1-2个优质idea，保质不求量：Seed 2: Reinforcement-Informed Demonstration Distillation for Noise-Robust VLA Training
Target: CoRL 2026 (Austin, Nov 9–12, 2026). Abstract deadline 2026-05-26 (12 days from today 2026-05-14); paper deadline 2026-05-29 (15 days).
Direction: RL-inspired experience scoring and filtering for VLA training data — methods that leverage data-intrinsic signals to identify and down-weight noisy, redundant, or suboptimal actions in real-world demonstration datasets before or during VLA fine-tuning. Real-world teleoperation data inevitably contains noise: hesitation pauses, corrective motions, grip fumbles, suboptimal trajectories, and redundant repeated actions. Standard behavioral cloning treats all timesteps equally, forcing the VLA to memorize noise as if it were signal — this is a fundamental source of brittleness. By borrowing the experience replay and advantage estimation machinery from offline RL, we can score each (state, action) pair by its contribution to task completion and filter or re-weight the training distribution accordingly. Unlike full offline RL (which replaces BC entirely), this approach retains the simplicity and stability of VLA fine-tuning while using RL-derived scores as a data curation signal. The key theoretical insight is that demonstration noise creates multi-modal action distributions at identical states, inflating the entropy of the learned policy; scoring and filtering collapses these modes to the high-performing subset, yielding a sharper, more robust policy.
Recent landscape (do not duplicate): Behavior Cloning, OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model, FT-NCFM: An Influence-Aware Data Distillation Framework for Efficient VLA Models, PLD: Probe, Learn, Distill – Self-Improving Vision-Language-Action Models with Data Generation via Residual RL, REDI: Refined Policy Distillation: From VLA Generalists to RL Experts, GOLD: Guided Offline Learning from Demonstrations, SHS: An Offline Reinforcement Learning Algorithm Based on Selection of High-Quality Samples, PER: Prioritized Experience Replay, PRGS: Peak Reward Guided Trajectory Segmentation, What Can RL Bring to VLA Generalization? An Empirical Study, πRL: πRL: Manifold Policy Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
Contribution type: METHOD ONLY. A two-stage demonstration distillation pipeline: (1) Temporal Advantage Scoring — train a lightweight value function on the demonstration data itself (using hindsight relabeling: final task success as sparse reward, or dense reward from state-goal distance) to compute per-timestep advantage estimates; actions with negative advantage (worse than the trajectory's average) are flagged as noisy; (2) Curriculum-Weighted Fine-Tuning — use the advantage scores as per-sample weights during VLA fine-tuning, with a curriculum that starts permissive (all data) and progressively sharpens to high-advantage subsets; (3) Consistency Regularization — for state-action pairs with high variance across similar states, add a consistency loss that encourages the VLA to commit to the high-scoring mode. No real robot required — the scoring is derived entirely from the existing dataset's structure.
EVAL PROTOCOL — IMPORTANT:
TRAIN on standard LIBERO suites (Object/Spatial/Goal/Long/90), with synthetic noise injection to simulate real-world demonstration noise (action jitter, redundant sub-trajectories, random pauses).
EVALUATE on existing LIBERO-PLUS / LIBERO-PRO style perturbation benchmarks (and similar community-released robustness benchmark series). DO NOT spend time constructing your own robustness benchmark — use existing perturbation suites and route the budget into the method.
Report robustness gap (Δ between nominal LIBERO success and perturbed-suite success) AND nominal preservation (must not regress on base LIBERO).
Additionally report: performance under varying noise injection ratios (10%/30%/50% noisy demonstrations), ablation of scoring function choices (MC return, TD advantage, trajectory ranking), and data efficiency curves (how much noisy data can be tolerated).
Experiments can be extended to other benchmarks with noisy demonstration collection (e.g., RLBench with injected perturbations).
SIM-ONLY MITIGATION: Using sim demonstrations with controlled noise injection is methodologically clean and well-accepted at CoRL. The scoring method is agnostic to sim/real — it operates on (state, action) pairs.
HARD CONSTRAINTS:
Compute: ≤200 H100-hours total. Fine-tune from open VLA checkpoints (OpenVLA, SmolVLA, OpenPi, π0) — no pretraining. Value function is lightweight (small MLP head). Show the math.
Time: ≤20 days. Build on OpenVLA, OpenPi and other proper codebases, LeRobot, HF Transformers.
Eval datasets: LIBERO base (training/nominal eval) + LIBERO-PLUS / LIBERO-PRO and similar existing perturbation suites (perturbed eval). No custom benchmark construction.
Look for: temporal advantage estimation from demonstration data without environment interaction, hindsight relabeling strategies for sparse-reward scoring, curriculum learning schedules that progressively filter noisy samples, connections between action distribution entropy and robustness, offline RL value estimation adapted to VLA's representation space. Avoid: requiring environment interaction or online rollouts (must be purely offline), full offline RL replacing BC (too unstable for VLA scale), simple trajectory-level success filtering (too coarse — need timestep-level scoring), just-add-noise training without filtering mechanism.

## LIBERO-Plus: A Robustness Benchmark for VLA Models

Visual–Language–Action (VLA) models report impressive success rates exceeding 95% on robotic manipulation benchmarks, yet these results may mask fundamental weaknesses in robustness.

### Key Findings

Models exhibit extreme sensitivity to perturbation factors, including camera viewpoints and robot initial states, with performance dropping from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations. The study introduces controlled perturbations across seven dimensions: objects layout, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, light conditions, background textures and sensor noise.

### Benchmark Overview

LIBERO-Plus is a comprehensive benchmark designed to establish a rigorous leaderboard for evaluating generalization capabilities across the key vulnerability dimensions identified in the study. The benchmark construction follows a systematic two-stage process: expanding the original LIBERO benchmark through seven distinct perturbation factors, followed by task filtering and category balancing based on empirical findings, and then evaluating the resulting tasks using four representative models and stratifying them into five difficulty levels (Level-1 to Level-5) according to observed accuracy distributions.

### Notable Findings

Models are largely insensitive to language variations, with further experiments revealing that models tend to ignore language instructions completely. Current VLA models lack compositional generalization capabilities, as their learned representations are entangled and cannot handle the complex, multi-dimensional perturbations that characterize real-world environments.

Filtered Behavioral Cloning (FBC) compares demonstrations to discard or down-weight the advice of sub-optimal policies. The advantage function is used as a reasonable metric for comparison, defined as the change in expected return when taking an action instead of following the current policy.

## VLA Models and Behavioral Cloning

Recent research on Vision-Language-Action models shows significant developments in 2025-2026. By leveraging vision-language models pretrained on internet-scale data and further training on large, heterogeneous robot demonstration datasets, VLAs can interpret sensor observations and natural language instructions to directly map them to robot actions.

VLA model training predominantly relies on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) through behavioral cloning of demonstration labels. However, RL fine-tuning is increasingly being applied to VLAs, with approaches ranging from incorporating human feedback to using offline RL updates or algorithms like PPO, sometimes in multi-stage processes with imitation learning.

Existing state-of-the-art methods for policy learning face significant limitations when expert demonstrations are low quality, and often require the filtering or reweighting of failed or noisy demonstrations. # ARFM: Key Details Extraction

## Full Abstract
"Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models based on flow matching have shown excellent performance in general-purpose robotic manipulation tasks. However, the action accuracy of these models on complex downstream tasks is unsatisfactory. One important reason is that these models rely solely on the post-training paradigm of imitation learning, which makes it difficult to have a deeper understanding of the distribution properties of data quality, which is exactly what Reinforcement Learning (RL) excels at. In this paper, we theoretically propose an offline RL post-training objective for VLA flow models and induce an efficient and feasible offline RL fine-tuning algorithm -- Adaptive Reinforced Flow Matching (ARFM). By introducing an adaptively adjusted scaling factor in the VLA flow model loss, we construct a principled bias-variance trade-off objective function to optimally control the impact of RL signal on flow loss. ARFM adaptively balances RL advantage preservation and flow loss gradient variance control, resulting in a more stable and efficient fine-tuning process."

## Answers Based on Abstract Content

**(1) Weighting approach:** ARFM employs "an adaptively adjusted scaling factor" rather than per-timestep weighting—a global mechanism for controlling RL signal influence.

**(4) Benchmarks:** The abstract mentions "simulation and real-world experimental results" but provides no specific benchmark names.

## RobustVLA: Multi-Modal Adversarial Training for Vision-Language-Action Models

RobustVLA focuses on robustness in all modalities and regularizes the objective to maintain consistent output actions across diverse input perturbations.

**Key Technical Approach:**

The method frames the problem as a multi-armed bandit and employs the upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm to select the most harmful perturbation for training. Additionally, for output robustness, the approach performs offline robust optimization against worst-case action noise that maximizes mismatch in flow matching objective.

**Experimental Results:**

On LIBERO, RobustVLA delivers absolute gains over baselines of 12.6% on the π₀ backbone and 10.4% on the OpenVLA backbone across all 17 perturbations, achieving 50.6x faster inference than existing visual-robust BYOVLA that requires external LLMs, and a 10.4% gain under mixed perturbations.

On the real-world FR5 robot, under four types of multimodal perturbations, RobustVLA shows strong low-data performance, outperforming π₀ by 65.6% success rate with 25 demonstrations.

## Summary of VACO

VACO is a novel bi-level framework that seamlessly integrates an inner loop for weighted supervised behavior cloning (BC) with an outer loop dedicated to value alignment.

### Framework Components

In this framework, the inner loop employs a meta-scoring network to evaluate and appropriately weight each training sample, while the outer loop maximizes value estimation for alignment with controlled noise to facilitate limited exploration.

## Overview

CUPID is a data curation method for robot imitation learning that uses influence functions to measure the causal impact of a demonstration on the policy's closed-loop performance. The paper was accepted to CoRL 2025.

## Core Methodology

CUPID estimates the influence of a training demonstration on the policy's expected return, which enables ranking and selection of demonstrations according to their impact on the policy's closed-loop performance. CUPID uses influence functions to predictively answer counterfactual questions about the effect of each demonstration on downstream policy performance without needing to retrain any policies.

## Applications

The approach curates data by filtering out training demonstrations that harmed the policy's performance and subselecting newly collected trajectories that will most help improve the policy.

## Results

Additionally, hardware experiments show that the method can identify robust strategies under distribution shift, isolate spurious correlations, and even enhance the post-training of generalist robot policies.

# Analysis of Advantage-Filtered Behavioral Cloning Paper

## Full Abstract
"Recent Offline Reinforcement Learning methods have succeeded in learning high-performance policies from fixed datasets of experience. A particularly effective approach learns to first identify and then mimic optimal decision-making strategies. Our work evaluates this method's ability to scale to vast datasets consisting almost entirely of sub-optimal noise. A thorough investigation on a custom benchmark helps identify several key challenges involved in learning from high-noise datasets. We re-purpose prioritized experience sampling to locate expert-level demonstrations among millions of low-performance samples. This modification enables offline agents to learn state-of-the-art policies in benchmark tasks using datasets where expert actions are outnumbered nearly 65:1."

## Key Findings

**Challenges Identified:**
The paper conducts a detailed examination that "identify[s] several key challenges involved in learning from high-noise datasets," indicating that advantage filtering faces substantial obstacles when confronted with predominantly sub-optimal training data.

**Proposed Solution:**
Rather than finding advantage filtering inherently effective, the authors propose a mitigation strategy: they "re-purpose prioritized experience sampling to locate expert-level demonstrations among millions of low-performance samples." This adaptation addresses the fundamental difficulty of identifying quality demonstrations within noisy data.

**Performance Achievement:**
The modified approach achieves strong results—enabling agents to reach state-of-the-art performance in benchmark tasks even when expert actions comprise only ~1.5% of the dataset (65:1 ratio).

In summary, the paper identifies fundamental challenges with standard advantage filtering in high-noise settings and proposes a sampling-based solution to mitigate these problems.

## ARFM: Adaptive Offline RL Post-Training for VLA Flow Models

The paper proposes Adaptive Reinforced Flow Matching (ARFM), an offline RL post-training objective for VLA flow models and an efficient offline RL fine-tuning algorithm.

### Key Technical Approach

ARFM controls the strength of the RL signal by introducing an adaptively adjusted scaling factor in the VLA flow loss function, aiming to preserve the RL signal (samples with higher RL advantage are amplified in the data distribution) while controlling the flow matching loss gradient variance (avoiding excessive gradient variance and training crashes).

### Weighting Strategy

The method theoretically constructs an energy-weighted flow matching loss with adaptive scaling factor, aiming to balance the RL signal and gradient variance on the data samples. The weighting is done at the sample level through the adaptive scaling factor rather than per-timestep or per-sample weighting in the traditional sense—instead, it adjusts how much the RL advantage influences individual samples during training.

### Results

ARFM adaptively balances RL advantage preservation and flow loss gradient variance control, resulting in a more stable and efficient fine-tuning process. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world robot manipulation tasks show that ARFM exhibits state-of-the-art generalization ability, robustness to dynamic perturbations, and excellent performance in few-shot and continuous learning scenarios.

# Technical Analysis of ARFM: Adaptive Offline RL Post-Training for VLA Flow Models

## 1. Sample Weighting Strategy
ARFM uses **global, batch-level scaling** rather than per-timestep weighting. The method applies a single adaptive scaling factor α to all samples in a batch:

> "wi(α)=exp(αR∗(Ati,ot))∑jexp(αR∗(Atj,ot))" 

This creates softmax weights across the entire batch based on standardized RL advantages, making the weighting trajectory/batch-global rather than temporally granular.

## 2. Value Function Architecture
ARFM is **critic-free**. It doesn't learn a separate value function. Instead, it uses standardized return-to-go advantages:

> "we are inspired by it to design a critic-free offline RL advantage signal for the VLA multi-task setting"

The advantages come from "Leave-One-Out" estimation within the data itself, not from pretrained VLA features or learned critics.

## 3. Problem Formulation
ARFM targets **general performance improvement**, not specifically noisy demonstrations. The paper states the core motivation is that imitation learning alone fails on complex downstream tasks, and offline RL can better exploit data quality distributions.

## 4. Adaptive Scaling Factor Details
α is a **single global hyperparameter per training batch**, not per-sample. It's computed via bisection iteration:

> "α∗=√(x∗)/σR where 4√x∗e^(2x∗)−2√x∗e^(x∗)−λσR/σL²=0"

The algorithm solves this nonlinear equation fresh each batch using Algorithm 1.

## 5. Benchmarks
- **LIBERO** (simulation): 4 suites (Object, Long, Spatial, Goal) with 10 tasks each
- **UR5 robot** (real-world): Pick-and-place with external perturbations
- Evaluation metrics: Success rate, robustness to action noise (0.1–0.3), few-shot learning, continuous learning

## 6. Architecture Compatibility
ARFM is **specifically designed for flow-matching VLAs** (tested on π0). The paper explicitly notes:

> "our adaptive offline RL post-training theoretical analysis and the induced fine-tuning algorithm can be applied but not limited to the π0 model"

It is **not evaluated on autoregressive models** like OpenVLA. Baseline comparisons show OpenVLA achieves 76.5% vs. ARFM's 92.1%, but ARFM doesn't fine-tune autoregressive architectures.

# Summary of "Learning from the Best: Smoothness-Driven Metrics for Data Quality in Imitation Learning"

## Full Abstract
The paper proposes RINSE (Ranking and INdexing Smooth Examples), a framework for scoring demonstrations in behavioral cloning based on trajectory smoothness rather than reinforcement learning-based advantage metrics. The method uses two complementary metrics: Spectral Arc Length (SAL) for frequency-domain regularity and Trajectory-Envelope Distance (TED) for spatial geometric deviation with contact awareness. Results show significant improvements on RoboMimic benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks.

## Approach: Smoothness vs. Advantage-Based Filtering
This work uses **smoothness-driven metrics**, distinctly different from RL-based advantage scoring. Rather than training policies to estimate trajectory value, RINSE grounds its approach in motor control theory, treating smoothness as "a hallmark of skilled movement." The method operates on raw trajectory data without requiring policy training loops.

## Benchmarks
- RoboMimic benchmarks
- Real-world manipulation tasks
- LIBERO-10 (when integrated with STRAP retrieval framework)

## Scope
The approach is **general to imitation learning**, not specific to Vision Language Models (VLAs). It's architecture-agnostic and applicable across behavioral cloning settings, particularly effective in "noisy or heterogeneous data regimes."

## DemInf Overview

DemInf (Demonstration Information Estimation) is an unsupervised method for curating robot demonstration datasets by using mutual information between states and actions as a proxy for data quality. Researchers from Google DeepMind Robotics and Stanford University developed DemInf, an unsupervised, offline method that estimates mutual information between states and actions to curate robot demonstration datasets.

## Method and Technical Approach

The Demonstration Information Estimation (DemInf) method is proposed for computationally estimating mutual information. The technique is based on k-nearest neighbor estimates of mutual information on top of simple VAE embeddings of states and actions. The method applies the KSG k-nearest-neighbor based mutual information estimator using latent representations, and finally filters demonstrations based on their estimated mutual information.

## Performance Results

On RoboMimic tasks, DemInf-filtered data results in 5-10% improvements in success rates compared to training on all available data, and real-world experiments on ALOHA and Franka systems confirm these improvements translate to physical robot performance.

## RSS 2025 Connection

The paper is published in the Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) conference proceedings. The paper was authored by Joey Hejna, Suvir Mirchandani, Ashwin Balakrishna, Annie Xie, Ayzaan Wahid, Jonathan Tompson, Pannag Sanketi, Dhruv Shah, Coline Devin, and Dorsa Sadigh.

## VLA-OPD: Bridging Offline SFT and Online RL for Vision-Language-Action Models

VLA-OPD is a unified post-training framework that bridges SFT and RL by leveraging dense, token-level supervision on self-generated trajectories, effectively resolving the exposure bias of SFT and the sample inefficiency of sparse-reward RL.

### Core Problem Addressed
Standard offline Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) suffers from distribution shifts and catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained capabilities, while online Reinforcement Learning (RL) struggles with sparse rewards and poor sample efficiency.

### Key Technical Innovation
Rather than relying on sparse environmental rewards, VLA-OPD leverages an expert teacher to provide dense, token-level supervision on the student's self-generated trajectories. The framework formulates a Reverse-KL distillation objective for VLA models, with a bounded mode-seeking property that effectively filters out the teacher's epistemic uncertainty while maintaining action diversity, preventing both entropy explosion of Forward-KL and premature entropy collapse of Hard-CE.

### Results
Experiments on LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0 benchmarks demonstrate that VLA-OPD significantly improves sample efficiency over RL and robustness over SFT, while effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting during post-training.

## Quality over Quantity (QoQ) - Demonstration Curation via Influence Functions

Quality over Quantity (QoQ) is a grounded and systematic approach to identifying high-quality data by defining data quality as the contribution of each training sample to reducing loss on validation demonstrations.

### Core Method

The approach leverages influence functions, which quantify the impact of individual training samples on model performance. Two key techniques adapt influence functions for robot demonstrations: (i) using maximum influence across validation samples to capture the most relevant state-action pairs, and (ii) aggregating influence scores of state-action pairs within the same trajectory to reduce noise and improve data coverage.

### Application to Robot Learning

Learning from demonstrations has emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end robot control, particularly when scaled to diverse and large datasets. However, the quality of demonstration data, often collected through human teleoperation, remains a critical bottleneck for effective data-driven robot learning. Human errors, operational constraints, and teleoperator variability introduce noise and suboptimal behaviors, making data curation essential yet largely manual and heuristic-driven.

### Experimental Results

By considering the true effect to the policy in data curation, QoQ substantially outperforms baseline methods that rely on state and action features up to 23.2% in Robomimic simulation and 30.0% in real robot success rate.

### Related Work

The search also revealed a related method called CUPID, which is a data curation method for robot imitation learning that uses influence functions to estimate the causal impact of each demonstration on a policy's closed-loop performance. Training with less than 33% of curated data can yield state-of-the-art diffusion policies on the simulated RoboMimic benchmark, with similar gains observed in hardware.

## Adaptive Q-Chunking Overview

Adaptive Q-Chunking (AQC) is an offline-to-online RL method that adapts chunk sizes per state through a principled advantage-based criterion. 

## The Core Problem and Solution

Offline-to-online reinforcement learning with action chunking eliminates multi-step off-policy bias and enables temporally coherent exploration, but all existing methods use a fixed chunk size across every state, which is suboptimal: near contact events the agent needs short chunks for reactive control, while during free-space motion long chunks provide better credit assignment.

AQC resolves both failures by comparing the advantage of each chunk size relative to a per-horizon baseline, normalized by the discount factor.

## VLA Application

The approach naturally extends to enhancing vision-language-action (VLA) models, where the VLA natively outputs action chunks; AQC scores multiple candidate chunks at each scale and selects the best prefix via the per-scale advantage criterion, giving the VLA reactive control near contacts while preserving smooth motion in free space, all without modifying the underlying model.

## Experimental Results

AQC achieves state-of-the-art offline and online success rates on OGBench and Robomimic, and can be applied to enhance the performance of large-scale VLA models that predict action sequences, significantly boosting performance on RoboCasa-GR1 tasks.

The paper was recently published on arXiv in May 2026 and represents an advancement in making offline-to-online RL more effective for both traditional control tasks and modern vision-language-action models.

## Overview

This work proposes a filter-and-restore framework, Diffusion-Model-Based Demonstration Restoration (DMDR), for imitation learning from noisy demonstrations.

## The Problem

Expert demonstrations often contain imperfections caused by errors from human experts or sensor/control system inaccuracies.

## The Approach

The proposed method first filters clean samples from the demonstrations and then learns conditional diffusion models to recover the noisy ones. More specifically:

- In the demonstration filtering stage, autoencoders are trained and the local outlier factor is performed using the learned embeddings to assign a pseudo label to each data point.

- In the demonstration restoration stage, a pair of conditional diffusion models is trained using the pseudo-labels. One conditional diffusion model aims to restore actions based on the corresponding states, while another diffusion model focuses on the reverse, restoring states based on actions.

## Results

The framework was evaluated in various domains, including robot arm manipulation, dexterous manipulation, and locomotion. The experiment results show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms existing methods across all the tasks. The paper was published on October 16, 2025.

## V-GPS: Value-Guided Policy Steering

V-GPS is a novel approach that improves the performance of pre-trained generalist robotic policies by re-ranking their actions at deployment time based on a value function learned via offline RL (e.g. Cal-QL).

### Key Features

The same single value function can be combined with any off-the-shelf generalist policy in a plug-and-play manner, without the need to fine-tune or access the policy's weights, improving downstream performance across multiple robotic platforms.

### Value Function Training

The repository includes the code for training the language-conditioned Cal-QL value function, as well as the code for combining it with the Octo model for test-time action sampling and evaluation on the SIMPLER simulated environment. Calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL) is preferred for training the value function due to its robustness to noisy actions and its ability to provide a conservative estimate of the optimal Q-value, which is crucial for the re-ranking process.

### Test-Time Action Reranking

Upon deployment, the method functions by sampling multiple action candidates from the generalist policy and evaluating these using the trained value function. Greedy selection: Choosing the action with the highest Q-value. Probabilistic sampling: Utilizing a softmax over the Q-values to maintain a balance between exploration and exploitation.

### Performance Results

V-GPS improves the success rates of all five generalist policies across multiple embodiments on average. The same single value function trained on cross-embodiment data is used for all policies across both real-world and simulated tasks.

### Publication

The paper was published at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in 2024, authored by Mitsuhiko Nakamoto, Oier Mees, Aviral Kumar, and Sergey Levine.
